theme: When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 126. You read this psalm in Unit 13 as a hope for the exiles. Now that the first exiles are home, read it again as their own song, sung with the foundation of the temple in front of them.
settingTheScene: Psalm 126 is a Song of Ascents. Earlier, you read it as a dream of return. Today read it as a song of those who have returned. The joy of verses 1 to 3 is the joy of the day the decree was announced. The prayer of verses 4 to 6 fits the days of delay, opposition, and small beginnings that you have just read in Ezra. It holds both: thanks for what God has done, and a plea for more.
observation: “When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream” (v. 1).
“Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy” (v. 2).
“Then they said among the nations, The LORD has done great things for them” (v. 2).
“The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad” (v. 3).
“Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!” (v. 4).
“Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!” (v. 5).
“He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing” (v. 6).
“Shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him” (v. 6).
interpretation:
The psalm is a song of already and not yet. In the first half, the people remember the day God restored them. It was so wonderful that it felt like a dream. Laughter, shouts of joy, and even the nations noticing. Ezra 1 and 3 are a commentary on this: a pagan king’s decree, the singing at the foundation. They were glad.

But in the second half, there is a request. “Restore our fortunes, O LORD.” The returned exiles are back, and yet they still pray for restoration. The land was poor, the walls were broken, the Persians ruled, and the opposition was strong. The first restoration was real, and the work was incomplete. They prayed for more, like the desert streams of the Negeb that burst into life after rain.

Then comes the image of sowing. The farmer goes out weeping because seed is precious, and in a time of famine, it hurts to put it in the ground. He sows in tears, trusting that it will grow. And God promises that he will come back with shouts of joy and with sheaves. The pattern is that tears and joy are connected. Tears are not wasted. They are part of the sowing.

This is what the returned community needed to hear while building the temple under threat. And it is what believers need while waiting for a final restoration. We have tasted the first fruits, and we wait for the harvest. We sow in tears because we live in a world that is not yet made new, and we do it in hope.
connection: Jesus said, “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). John 16:20: “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.” Galatians 6:9: “In due season we will reap, if we do not give up.” 1 Corinthians 15:58: “Your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” Romans 8:23-25 describes waiting for the redemption of our bodies. Revelation 21:4 promises no more tears.
application:
Name something you are currently “sowing in tears.” Offer it to God, and trust the harvest.

Thank God for a restoration he has already given you, and ask for more.

Encourage someone who is weeping as they work or serve.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the great things he has done for you.
Ask him to restore what is dry in you.
Tell him about tears you are sowing.
